Thought: Careful, unusually candid controlled study, but the headline finding (full text beats abstracts; strategies tie when all papers fit one prompt) is largely expected and is shown in a regime chosen so that direct reading should win. The regimes where strategy could matter (large relevant reference sets, retrieval) failed because of safety-filter stops or were run on 4-10 entries. Every measurement layer (fact splitting, present/absent marking, 'stated in text' judgement, audit) is done by the writer's own model family, with zero human validation, which is a serious gap for a paper whose first contribution is a benchmark. The reference is narrow: variant-centred ClinVar paragraphs, with only ~24% of a draft's statements having a counterpart. Differences among reading strategies (0.5-2 pp) are about the size of replicate noise, so the benchmark barely discriminates. Statistics, completion handling, the planted-error audit analysis and the corrected-analysis disclosure are good. Writing is extremely dense and hedged. Overall: a solid workshop or datasets-track paper, borderline-below the ICLR main-track bar. 5, Reject.
Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded writing of knowledge-base entries. It uses 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 cited references each). Every entry is drafted from exactly the papers its curators cited, with the causal gene withheld and each paper given at its open-access level (19% full text, 67% abstract, 14% title). One model (Claude Opus 5.5) runs six strategies: direct reading, an agentic curator, an evidence graph, case-table-first, recall-then-verify, and a memory-only control. Three add-ons are also tested: second-hand evidence from citing papers, a reconciled case database, and a learned curation guide. A shared claim-level audit with a repair round and shared guards apply to every strategy. The primary endpoint is 'OMIM facts conveyed': coverage of fixed fact lists that were split once from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar (6,652 facts over 476 paragraphs). Secondary endpoints are HPO synopsis F1, allelic-variant recall and precision, causal-gene F1 and inheritance agreement. The main findings are as follows. (i) Hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1% in 46 entries. (ii) On facts the supplied text is judged to state, three reading strategies convey 93.6-94.4% and lie within a point of one another; on unstated facts they convey under 7%, no more than the memory-only control. (iii) Case-table-first trails direct reading by about 2 points, which a matched ablation partly attributes to extraction effort. (iv) Released PaperQA2 (10 entries) and GraphRAG (4 entries) pipelines, run on the same papers and model, convey fewer facts at higher cost; STORM could not run because the model's safety filter stopped its prompts. (v) Planted-error tests show that the audit catches swapped citations, moved sentences and single-value substitutions, but not added irrelevant citations, most broadened claims, or omissions. The paper also reports replicate and judge noise, a symmetric completion rule (after an earlier asymmetric analysis produced a spurious 2.1-point difference), padding with unrelated papers, an attempt at large entries, and a creation-date contamination check.
Strengths: Clean experimental control. Papers, model, guards, audit and scoring are fixed, and only the generation strategy varies. Fixing the fact lists once, without sight of any draft, is a good design choice: it avoids the denominator drift of per-draft decomposition, which the authors show inflates levels by 2-5 points.

The within-paper hidden-full-text manipulation is a genuine causal test rather than an observational stratification. The effect is very large (about 44 points, higher with full text in every entry but one), so it is unlikely to be overturned by judge noise.

The statistical reporting is careful: paired bootstrap intervals over entries, sign tests with Holm adjustment for secondary measures, judge variation (95.7% per-fact agreement across judgings), and run-to-run replicate noise used as a yardstick separate from the test. Completion is treated as an outcome, with an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis.

The paper is unusually transparent. It reports null and negative results (learned guide, reconciliation, recall-then-verify) and discloses an earlier analysis whose asymmetric handling of stopped replies produced a spurious 2.1-point difference (Appendix I.4). The 'measurement lessons' (symmetric handling of stopped replies, fixed fact lists, per-paper audit verdicts) are practically useful to others building LLM-judged generation benchmarks.

The audit analysis is informative. It shows mechanistically why best-verdict aggregation over cited papers cannot detect over-citation (0/30 added citations flagged) and that omissions are invisible by construction. It also adds a completeness check and replays the stored audits to recover per-paper citation precision. This is a useful caution for FActScore-style claim-level evaluation of cited text.

Attributing missed facts to the available text (49% of missed full-text facts were stated in the text, versus 2% for abstract-only papers) and tracing conveyed facts to their provenance (only 1.7% of fully conveyed abstract-paper facts are stated in no supplied text) make the access argument concrete.

The benchmark is built from public resources. The authors release a harness with per-entry drafts, verdicts and scores, and handle rights for the curator text responsibly (fact identifiers, not wording).
Weaknesses: No human validation anywhere in the measurement chain. One model family writes, splits facts, marks facts present, partial, absent or contradicted, judges whether the supplied text 'states' each fact, and runs the audit. For a paper whose first contribution is a benchmark, the absence of even a small curator or expert check (e.g., a few hundred fact judgements or 'stated' judgements) is a major gap. Self-preference (Panickssery et al., 2024) could act differently on the different strategies' output styles, e.g., graph-writer versus direct-reading prose. Without any human anchor, the 0.5-2 point differences between strategies cannot be interpreted with confidence.

The headline conclusion is largely expected and shown in a regime that favours it. The entries have 2-12 references, a median of about 40k characters and only 19% full text, so all papers fit comfortably in one long-context prompt. In that regime, intermediate representations and agentic reading have little room to help, and a ceiling of about 94% on stated facts is unsurprising. The regimes where strategy could plausibly matter were not compared: large sets of relevant papers failed because of safety-filter stops (0 of 4 large entries comparable), and retrieval without the reference list was run on 10 entries with one strategy. The padding test adds unrelated papers that the model trivially ignores (no draft cited one), so it does not test crowding. Consequently, 'access, not strategy, limits agreement' is supported only for the easy regime, which the authors acknowledge but which limits the significance.

The benchmark discriminates weakly. Among the reading strategies the differences on the primary endpoint are 0.5-1.9 points, against a replicate-noise half-width of 1.0 point. Two of the three intervals include or touch zero, and the case-table-first sign test is p = 0.071. A benchmark on which all reasonable reading strategies tie may have limited value for guiding system design, unless it is extended to harder regimes or to more models.

The reference is narrow and indirect. The primary endpoint uses OMIM's variant-centred allelic-variant paragraphs (from gene entries, via ClinVar), not the phenotype-entry narrative the drafts are meant to emulate. Only about 24% of a draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference, and drafts make about twice as many statements per paper as the paragraph has facts. Absolute levels (about 49%) are therefore hard to interpret, and most draft content is checked only by the same-model audit, i.e., for fidelity rather than correctness.

Single proprietary model, with idiosyncratic failures. All results are for Claude Opus 5.5, called through a CLI without temperature or seed control. Opaque safety-filter stops removed entries unevenly, prevented STORM from running at all, and blocked the large-entry experiment. Several conclusions (e.g., about released systems and large inputs) are therefore partly conclusions about this model's filter. No second model family is tested, even as a judge.

The released-system comparison is weak. PaperQA2 was run without its agent, because the adapter lacks function calling. GraphRAG was run on only 4 entries, which admit no test. Both answered six section questions rather than writing an entry natively, used one small local embedding model, and were run at one setting. The authors' strategies went through the repair round and the systems did not. The authors appropriately caveat that this is not a ranking, but this makes the contribution-(2) claim about released pipelines thin.

Strategy versus implementation is confounded. The matched ablation shows that extraction effort alone moves case-table-first by about 2 points, the same size as its deficit. Paradigm-level conclusions are therefore hard to separate from implementation choices; different, equally reasonable implementations of the graph or agent could plausibly shift the ordering.

Several second-round experiments were cut to about a third of their design size and some ended below even that (Appendix J). As a result, many secondary claims rest on 2-10 entries or 2-30 items per class. This is appropriately labelled exploratory, but it adds breadth without adding much evidence.

Contamination is only partially controlled. The memory-only control conveys about 15% overall, and abstract-only direct-reading coverage falls from 49.8% to 37.9% between older and newer bands, so memory likely helps reading on older entries. The 2026 held-out set has only 20 compared entries and five strategies.

Presentation is very dense. Nearly every sentence carries several numbers, intervals, sample sizes and hedges. The abstract and introduction are hard to parse ('means over entries', 'no arm repaired', 'stopped replies'), and important design details (the reference's scope, what 'stated' means, the completion rule) require repeated cross-referencing to the 30-page appendix. A clearer separation between core and exploratory results in the main text would help considerably.
Questions: Could you provide even a small human validation, e.g., a domain expert or curator re-judging a random sample of fact marks (present/partial/absent), 'stated in text' judgements and audit verdicts? This would show whether the 0.5-2 point strategy differences are within judge error, and how often 'contradicted' facts reflect true draft errors rather than reference or judgement errors (Appendix I.3 suggests the model often sides with the draft).

Would rejudging the existing drafts and fact lists with a different model family (only the judge, not the writer) change the ordering of reading strategies? This would be inexpensive relative to the full study and would directly address self-preference.

Can you characterise what triggers the safety-filter stops (topic, paper content, chain-of-thought prompts)? Could the large-entry and STORM experiments be run through a direct API, or with a second model, so that the regime in which strategies might separate becomes testable?

In the regime tested, direct reading sees all papers in one prompt. Have you considered forcing a context budget (e.g., capping the prompt at a fraction of total input), so that retrieval or intermediate representations become necessary? That would test the 'access versus strategy' claim where strategy has room to matter.

How sensitive is the primary endpoint to fact-splitting granularity and to the half-credit for 'partly present'? Do the 'fully conveyed' figures in the appendix change any conclusion about the strategy ordering?

Given that only about 24% of draft statements have a reference counterpart, what fraction of the remaining statements would a curator consider correct and appropriate for the entry? Is the 96% 'judged supported' rate informative about correctness, given that the auditor is the writer's model family?

Why is the primary endpoint not adjusted for the five strategy-versus-direct-reading comparisons, and how do you reconcile cases where the bootstrap interval excludes zero but the sign test does not (case table first)?
For PaperQA2, was it possible to provide function calling (e.g., through a different adapter) so that its agent could be evaluated, given that the agent is central to its published design?
Limitations: The authors list their limitations thoroughly: single model family, no human validation, a narrow reference, a given reference list, open-access text without supplements, a small 2026 set, uneven loss of entries to stopped replies, the few-reference regime, audit blind spots, and released systems at one setting each. I agree with all of them. The most consequential are the lack of any human validation of the judge and the untested large-reference regime, which together limit how far the 'strategy matters little' conclusion generalises.
An additional limitation is that the conclusions about paradigms rest on single in-house implementations whose details (e.g., extraction effort) move results by as much as the paradigm differences.
The authors appropriately note that generated entries are drafts for expert review, not clinical guidance, and must not be presented as OMIM content.
